title: US Retail Sales Post Steepest Monthly Drop Since May 2025
excerpt: Consumer spending fell 0.6% in July as Amazon Prime Day timing shift and lower gas prices dragged down receipts, defying forecasts of a small gain.
body:
• U.S. retail sales fell 0.6% in July, the steepest monthly decline since May 2025 and well below the 0.1% gain economists had forecast.
  • Online sales plunged 2.2% after Amazon moved its Prime Day event from July to June, pulling forward consumer demand.
  • Auto sales dropped 2% and gas station receipts fell 0.9%, though restaurant spending rose 0.5%.
  • Analysts say the pullback is likely temporary, with rising household wealth from a 14% S&P 500 rally this year expected to support spending.

American consumers pulled back sharply in July, with retail sales posting their biggest monthly decline in over a year as the effects of an early Amazon Prime Day and falling gasoline prices rippled through the data.

Retail sales dropped 0.6% last month after an unrevised 0.2% gain in June, the Commerce Department's Census Bureau reported on Friday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast a 0.1% increase, with estimates ranging from a 0.5% drop to a 0.7% gain.

What Drove the Decline

The biggest culprit was timing. Amazon pulled its annual Prime Day sale forward to June this year, creating a surge in online spending that month followed by a sharp reversal. Online retail sales fell 2.2% in July, the largest decline of any category.

Auto dealership sales dropped 2% after a strong June, while gas station receipts slid 0.9% as fuel prices declined. Even excluding gasoline, retail spending was still down 0.6%, suggesting the weakness extended beyond energy prices.

The so-called control group — which strips out autos, gasoline, building materials, and food services and feeds directly into GDP calculations — declined 0.44%, compared to the 0.4% gain economists had projected.

"American consumers are showing signs of fatigue. Some of the pullback in July is due to Amazon Prime Days, Walmart+ and Target Circle deals happening in June. But even with lower spending on gas in July, consumers weren't eager to spend elsewhere."

— Heather Long, Chief Economist, Navy Federal Credit Union

Temporary Setback or Turning Point

Economists largely characterized the decline as a timing-driven blip rather than a fundamental shift in consumer behavior. Generous tax refunds earlier this year had supported spending through the second quarter, but those have now been exhausted.

An analysis by PNC Financial found that households in July appeared more sensitive to rising gasoline prices than earlier in the year, creating what the bank called a "less supportive backdrop for spending in the second half." However, PNC economists said it was "difficult to envision a scenario where spending truly rolls over," given the substantial rise in household wealth.

The S&P 500 has climbed approximately 14% this year, boosting portfolio values and providing a cushion for upper-income consumers. Restaurant and bar spending rose 0.5% in July, indicating that services-sector demand remained intact even as goods purchases fell.

Broader Economic Context

Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of U.S. economic output, making the retail sales report a closely watched indicator of the economy's health. Over the past year, retail sales have still risen about 5%, somewhat above the long-term average.

The report lands ahead of upcoming Federal Reserve discussions on monetary policy. Markets have been watching for signs of consumer weakness that could influence the pace of future rate decisions.

David Rosenberg of Rosenberg Research noted the decline "could well be related to the timing of Amazon Prime Day and the vacuum created by the end of the World Cup," but added it "could be validation for the -23k contraction we saw in nonfarm payrolls last month."

Despite the weak headline number, major stock indexes were mostly calm on Friday, with the S&P 500 edging up 0.1% and on pace for a third consecutive week of gains.
